newsitem.title: UK: Clashing US/Japan rate expectations punish dollar.
newsitem.headline: Clashing US/Japan rate expectations punish dollar.

text.p: The dollar sank some two yen and one pfennig by European midsession, punished by increasingly divergent rate expectations for Japan and the United States.

As Japanese officials continued their verbal support for the yen, speculation also grew of a Japanese rate rise. Meanwhile, comments from U.S. Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan, while interpreted variously in the market, were seen by many as reducing the chances of Fed tightening later this month.
"Greenspan wasn't suggesting there was likely to be any more (tightening) very soon...On that basis the dollar's easier," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase here.

Greenspan said he expected economic growth to slow later this year, but the Fed would need to act were that not so. He noted scant evidence of an imminent inflation pick-up but argued labour markets were tight and the economy had little slack.

Some chose to focus on the fact Greenspan had talked at all of the possibility of U.S. tightening. Fed policymakers next meet on May 20, after hiking rates a quarter-point at their last meeting in late March.
"It's awakened people to the fact they could be putting rates up on May 20," said Pat Magill, head of the corporate desk at Daiwa Europe in London.
The dollar was quoted at 122.03/13 at 1051 GMT, off a session low of 121.73 but far beneath late Thursday's European level of 123.70/80.
Dollar/mark was cushioned slightly by a slide in mark/yen -- which sank to a low of 71.59 from late yesterday's 72.47/50 -- but also weakened, to touch a low of 1.6980.
The dollar recovered to 1.7009/14 marks by 1051 GMT, with the mark changing hands at 71.70/73 yen.
Traders said volume was extremely thin, amplifying exchange rate moves, as many continental European traders had extended Thursday's Ascension Day holiday into a long weekend.

The yen drew support from a Japanese press report which speculated on the chances of a discount rate rise there in July. Some in the Bank of Japan think its low interest rate policy should end soon, the Nikkei Kinyu story suggested.
An ongoing barrage of yen-positive comment from Japanese finance officials did the dollar no favours.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka expressed the hope that markets would "further digest" the G7 accord reached in April, when the group agreed to monitor forex developments and cooperate as appropriate in the markets. To be effective, intervention should be a joint effort, Mitsuzuka said.
Influential finance ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara -- who ambushed the dollar yesterday when he said it was possible it could drop to 103 yen -- sent another warning to the market.
Sakakibara, known in the markets as "Mr Yen", reiterated the oft-heard line that Japan would deal with excessive currency moves in a timely and decisive manner.
"It's clear Japanese officials are continuing to try to talk down the dollar," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
"The fact the dollar has weakened...suggests there's no need for them to intervene," he added.
This has been a week short on U.S. data -- none are due today -- and the market is highly vulnerable to officials' comments in the absence of concrete figures, analysts said.
Players must wait until Tuesday for new data clues on which way the Fed will swing, with U.S. April retail sales kicking off a batch of key numbers which includes PPI and CPI.

Elsewhere, the Swiss franc climbed as fears intensified of a broad-based European monetary union and a weak euro. The franc firmed to 1.4370/80 per dollar and 84.47/50 centimes per mark from late yesterday's European levels of 1.4445/55 and 84.50/51.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
